items.body: Blue Cross of Idaho has denied some medical claims for employees and dependents in Coeur d’Alene after school district leaders refused to sign a contract to make monthly payments to cover their portion the Idaho School Benefit Trust’s $13 million shortfall. But the district is still not signing the 12-month binding contract addendum, according to a letter Superintendent Shon Hocker sent to all district employees on Wednesday. The letter states the district learned that some employees have received claim denials or notices from Blue Cross, or their providers, for claims in July and August. “We understand and share the concern and frustration this may cause,” Hocker wrote to his employees. Trustees conducted an emergency meeting on Tuesday, which was not livestreamed or recorded, and voted to authorize the district to negotiate a “modified agreement that allows us to make monthly payments without compromising our legal standing.” “If a fair resolution cannot be reached quickly, the Board authorized the district to pay the full lump sum to ensure our employees’ claims are processed without delay,” Hocker wrote. items.body: With help from the Legislature, Idaho’s largest school district has the lowest property tax rate in the state and can build two new buildings over the next year without increasing its local tax burden. At a time when bonds and levies are hard to pass, West Ada School District trustees on Monday night approved a complicated loan agreement that will give the district $56.4 million in cash. The money will help the district turn a vacant warehouse into a career and technical education center on Locust Grove and rebuild Lake Hazel Elementary, with both projects expected to open in fall 2027. The district will pay the loan off over 15 years with ongoing state facilities funding. West Ada CFO Dave Roberts said the district expects at least $35.8 million in sales tax every year from House Bill 292 , passed in 2023. The bill was designed to reduce school districts’ property tax burden. A fraction of that annual appropriation, $5.3 million, will pay off the loan without increasing property taxes. “It’s possible that with this type of funding that West Ada may be able to build buildings without ever going to taxpayers again,” Roberts told EdNews on Tuesday. The projects follow the district’s recent completion of Independence Elementary in Star, which was built with state modernization funds from House Bill 521 and without an increase in property taxes. items.body: (UPDATED, 4:28 p.m., with comments from Marsing School District.) In a student survey last fall, 46% of Notus junior high school and high school students listed mental health as a concern. District Superintendent Jen Wright thought she had found a partial solution. She wanted to use $60,000 in federal grants to hire a behavioral health coordinator for preschool through 12 th grade. But last week, legislators tabled the program, leaving Notus and nine other rural schools shut out on funding. “I was really thinking that we were going to get it,” Wright said in an interview Tuesday. “It’s just very disappointing.” Until last week, the Department of Health and Welfare was pursuing a $1.2 million behavioral health hub program — designed to offer optional in-person or telehealth services to students and families. The money was going to come from a fraction of Idaho’s $186 million federal rural healthcare transformation grant . The Legislature’s Rural Health Transformation Committee abruptly put the behavioral health hub proposal on hold Friday — shifting the $1.2 million out of the program. Committee members noted that the Legislature had rejected a similar proposal in 2024 . Before Friday’s vote, nine districts had applied for behavioral health grants: Aberdeen, American Falls, Cascade, Castleford, Garden Valley, Marsing, Notus, Snake River and Wilder. Heritage Academy Public Charter in Jerome also applied. All the applicants were rural — and some distance from the closest clinic. In Notus’ case, the nearest mental health services are in Caldwell, a half hour drive away. Aberdeen School District Superintendent Scott Muir was hoping to use a $110,000 grant to bridge the gap between his rural community and health services in American Falls, about 20 minutes away, and Pocatello, about 50 minutes away. The grant would have gone toward new mental health and wellness services, additional counseling support and facilities upgrades. “We believe these efforts would have had a meaningful impact on the overall well-being of our students and community,” Muir said in an email to EdNews Tuesday. Friday’s committee vote came as a surprise to Wright. She said she only learned Notus had lost out on its grant through EdNews’ coverage of the hearing. The sudden news means Notus will look for other options. A new partnership with Insight Counseling — a third party that already works with Marsing and Wilder — will provide Notus with a clinical counselor. Without a $100,000 federal grant, American Falls will look at other ways to serve students and families in need, Superintendent Randy Jensen said Wednesday. “I also hope the state continues looking at more upstream approaches to student mental health and behavioral needs,” Jensen said. “If we can provide stronger support to children and families when students are younger, we may be able to prevent some of the more significant challenges that require intervention later. Prevention should be an important part of this conversation.” The Marsing School District applied for an $89,028 grant, and on Wednesday afternoon, Superintendent Norm Stewart called the committee’s decision ironic. “During the last legislative session, we were told that a state-mandated 60 seconds of silence would help positively impact student mental health. items.body: Idaho showed a 66% rise of 18 and 19-year-old registered voters between 2018 and 2022. Then, in 2023, Idaho legislators passed new voting laws targeted at student voters. After the laws took effect, Idaho saw a 23% decline in 18- and 19-year-old registered voters. Idaho is now last in the nation in the percentage of 18-year-old registered voters compared to registered voters aged 45 and older. Despite zero evidence of Idaho students fraudulently using their student IDs to vote, the law removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification. Previously, students could use their ID as a form of identification for registering to vote, and to vote on election day. BABE VOTE and the League of Women Voters of Idaho challenged the laws in court. However, our case was dismissed without a trial. If granted a trial, we would have shown evidence of legally eligible Idaho voters who were unable to vote under the new laws. Upon pushback from the community, Representative Brent Crane (R-Nampa) who helped pass the laws, said,“[the laws] were doing exactly what they were designed to do.” We continue to hear positive messages from our Secretary of State about how easy it is for Idahoans to register and vote. But for some legally eligible Idahoans, it has not been easy. Although these laws specifically targeted students, they have created barriers for other Idahoans—including people who have moved, changed their names, or no longer drive. Sam Sandmire, a BABE VOTE member, spent more than an hour on the phone with the Secretary of State’s staff troubleshooting the system as she tried to change her address on her voter registration. It took her more than a week and additional phone calls before she was able to request an absentee ballot. This is not a one-time occurrence. Many long-time voters have reported that they have been removed from the voter database, even though they have voted consistently in recent elections. So these are not hypothetical concerns. They are issues we are hearing about and experiencing ourselves. If voters are unaware of potential problems or delays, they may wait until it is too late to resolve them. BABE VOTE does not want to discourage anyone from registering or voting. Our goal is to warn legally eligible voters to start now: check your voter registration, register or re-register to vote, and make a plan to vote, whether by absentee ballot, early in person, or at the polls on Election Day. Idahoans should not have to navigate unnecessary obstacles to exercise their right to vote, but until those obstacles are addressed, voters need to know they exist. Voting should not be a last-minute scramble. Don’t wait until Election Day. Check your registration, make a plan, and give yourself time to resolve any problems so you can cast your ballot. Babe, VOTE! BABE VOTE is a non-partisan, non-profit that empowers young people to organize their communities for democracy.

items.body: Idaho State Treasurer Julie Ellsworth, left, and Democratic challenger Kevin Jones. (Photos courtesy of candidates) Two candidates will vie for the position to manage Idaho’s cash flow and investments, and they offer differing views on how to do so. Incumbent Republican Treasurer Julie Ellsworth will face Democratic challenger Kevin Jones in the Nov. 3 general election. Jones, although running as a Democrat, believes the position should be nonpartisan and has announced he will unaffiliated the day after the election. The treasurer’s office serves as the state’s chief financial officer — which includes overseeing the receipt of state money, accounting for disbursement of funds, investing idle state money, and administering the unclaimed property program , the 529 College Savings Fund, and the Idaho ABLE savings accounts. Each of the candidates are focused on the state’s investment strategy, but with different approaches and metrics for success. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT Who are the candidates seeking office for Idaho treasurer? Jones , 63, said he is running to improve the state’s investment yields and said his background better suits him to the job. He previously ran Boise-based Harmonic Investment Advisors. He is a longtime institutional portfolio manager and a chartered financial analyst, which is an internationally recognized professional certification for advanced investment management and financial analysis, he said. “I’m a very logical individual, and I’m also a former college golfer, so I’ve spent my entire life competing, where numbers matter more than how someone dresses, what party they’re in, and so forth,” Jones said. “… You either post the score on the golf course, or you don’t. You either do well at managing investment portfolios, or you don’t.” Idaho’s 2026 election voter pamphlet is coming to a mailbox near you Ellsworth , 64, was first elected as state treasurer in 2018 after serving 12 years non-consecutively as an Idaho state representative. She has been a public school teacher, and a mediator and business consultant. She said she wants to run again because her work has helped the state. “I think I’m doing a good job, and I can see that it elevates Idahoans,” Ellsworth said. “It’s very uplifting. The main focus of my job is to assure that money is safe in the state of Idaho, that it is collected in a uniform manner. … and then when money is going to be spent but is idle at the time, we invest it. And I love turning money back to Idaho taxpayers.” How would the candidates manage Idaho investments? When the state has funds that aren’t yet ready to be spent, the treasurer’s office can invest the money to try and grow the fund until it’s ready to be spent. The Treasurer Investment Advisory Board reviews policies and performance of funds, and private firms that contract with the state help oversee investments with the treasurer. Jones said the state’s portfolios have been underperforming. He highlighted recent reports from the investment advisory board showing state funds, such as the IDLE fund , producing total returns less than a comparable index fund. An index fund tracks performance of a certain index — or group of investments that often have something in common — and tries to mimic it through buying a representative sample of stocks and bonds in that index. items.body: The Senate has overwhelmingly endorsed a far-reaching and bipartisan bill to overhaul college sports. Idaho Republican Sens. Mike Crapo and Jim Risch both voted for the Protect College Sports Act of 2026 , which passed Monday on a 77-22 vote . The bill still allows “revenue sharing,” direct payments to athletes. The spending cap would increase from $21.5 million to roughly $49 million, ESPN reported . Other provisions of the bill would allow student-athletes to transfer only once in their college careers; cap fees to agents at 5%; and restrict colleges and universities from cutting programs in Olympic sports in order to sink the savings into football. “College athletics are facing significant challenges Congress can and must meaningfully address,” Crapo said in a news release Tuesday. “The Protect College Sports Act provides much-needed clarity and consistency for student athletes and higher education institutions.” In the same news release, Idaho’s three university presidents took turns hailing the bill. “The Protect College Sports Act is an important pathway for creating a stable, fair foundation for college athletics,” Boise State University President David Hahn said. Despite the overwhelming Senate vote — and backing from President Donald Trump — the Protect College Sports Act is not a done deal. It still needs to pass the House, which is on recess until after the November election. If the House fails to act on the bill during a lame-duck session after the elections, ESPN noted, the process would have to start over in the next congressional session. items.body: Susan Hinchcliffe, a volunteer with the Corrales Fire Department, gives Rachel Ralya’s 14-month old son a Moderna COVID-19 vaccine on June 23, 2022, following the FDA authorization of the vaccine for children ages 6 months to 5 years old. (Shelby Wyatt/Source NM) An Idaho judge dismissed a lawsuit from a Boise daycare and parents that sought to block enforcement of a state law that bans daycares from requiring vaccines or medical treatment. The lawsuit claimed that the Idaho Medical Freedom Act was unconstitutionally vague, arguing its language bans a range of routine health protections — including handwashing and sending home sick kids. But last week, Chief U.S. District Judge for the District of Idaho Amanda K. Brailsford granted Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador’s request to dismiss the lawsuit, which was brought by Le Soleil Child Care LLC, and three parents whose kids attend the daycare or hope to. In her ruling, the federal judge wrote she agreed with Labrador’s interpretation of the law’s definition of “medical interventions,” writing that they refer to health actions that are “medical in nature.” “The (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) plainly and unambiguously sets out a standard of prohibited conduct that gives a person of ordinary intelligence fair notice of what is prohibited,” Brailsford wrote, ruling that the daycare didn’t show that the state law was unconstitutionally vague. “The Court agrees with the AG that Le Soleil is free to promote its beliefs and values about public health and vaccinations …” the judge wrote. “The only thing the (Idaho Medical Freedom Act) prevents is Le Soleil requiring that only vaccinated students hear those values.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE AG praises court ruling. Parents, daycare consider appealing, lawyer says. The ruling upholds a state law that bans daycares, businesses, governments and schools from mandating vaccines or “medical interventions,” which are defined as: “a medical procedure, treatment, device, drug injection, medication, or medical action taken to diagnose, prevent, or cure a disease or alter the health or biological function of a person.” In a statement, Labrador said he was pleased with the court’s decision. “Parents make medical decisions for their children. A daycare does not,” Labrador said in a statement . “The Legislature protected that choice in the Medical Freedom Act, and the court upheld it. Daycares can tell parents what they believe about vaccines and health, but they cannot turn a child away because of a parent’s medical decision. That decision belongs to families, and I’m pleased the court agreed.” Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? The proposals on federal land in Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah and Wyoming were first reported last week by The Washington Sun, whose reporters reviewed difficult to find right-of-way requests via BLM’s Mineral and Land Records System . The bulk of federally managed land in the U.S. is in the West, including in Oregon where half the state’s land is owned and managed by the federal government. Oregon is among the top 10 markets for data centers in the U.S., according to Pew Research. Under the executive order, Trump mandated that federally owned land and resources be used for “the expeditious and orderly development of data centers (…) to be used in service of the prosperity and security of the American people.” It’s the first time the Bureau of Land Management, tasked with managing more than 245 million public acres for uses that include animal grazing, timber harvesting and recreation, has been ordered to include data centers in its portfolio. items.body: An independent conservative running in a swing district against a Republican incumbent and a Democratic challenger means anything could happen in November. Rep. Mike Pohanka, R-Jerome, narrowly won the 2024 general election over Democrat Ned Burns by 2.4 percentage points. Pohanka now faces a three-way race against a Democrat with a long career in education and a Christian conservative independent who believes the government has turned away from God. Pohanka is seeking a second term in District 26 House Seat A. District 26 includes blue voters in Blaine County and red voters to the south in Jerome and Lincoln counties. But Pohanka said he considers himself colorblind. He’s said he’s a public servant who wants to help his constituents. “I have people coming up to me saying, ‘You know what? I’m a Democrat, and I’m voting for you because you are a person that cares and you’re doing the job,'” Pohanka said. That attitude encouraged independent Bella Schiffler to run. She interned for two lawmakers in Boise and said she learned that many politicians who call themselves conservative aren’t really conservative. Schiffler said education has become “woke,” citing a debunked hoax about litter boxes in schools. She told EdNews that she would be in favor of taking away women’s right to vote if it helped the country move closer to God. “America is a Christian nation, and we are founded on godly principles,” Schiffler said. Pohanka said he hopes Schiffler will not split the conservative vote in November, which happened two years ago when her aunt, Kala Tate, ran for the Senate as an independent. Anita Janis, chair of the Jerome County Democrats, wants to bring her experiences of teaching around the country to the Legislature. She said Idaho can learn from other states, where education funding works differently. “I have lived in other states where there would never be a levy put together to support salaries,” Janis said. She wants to see the Legislature fulfill its duty under the Idaho Constitution to fund public schools. Election Day is Nov. 3. (Photo courtesy of Sarah Wood/U.S. Department of Energy) Editor’s Note: This is the first installment of a three-part Idaho Capital Sun series examining the proposal to bring a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Part one focuses on Gov. Brad Little’s role in negotiations and his priorities for Idaho. The series continues Monday and Tuesday with a closer look at the cases for and against bringing a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. Idaho Gov. Brad Little said he will not jeopardize the health of the Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer or the health of Idahoans as he continues to negotiate potentially bringing a new Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus to Idaho. “I’ve had this direct conversation with Secretary (of Energy Chris) Wright: Disposal of spent fuel over the aquifer in Idaho – that’s a nonstarter,” Little said in an interview Wednesday at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. In July, U.S. Department of Energy officials announced that Idaho is one of five states selected as a finalist to host one of the new innovation campuses. Little signed a memorandum of understanding in July with the U.S. Department of Energy, or DOE, to hold formal discussions and negotiations about bringing an innovation campus to Idaho. The Eastern Snake Plain Aquifer is outlined in orange of this map of Washington, Oregon and Idaho. (Map courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey) If Idaho is selected as a host site, the federal government has said the state will have to accept shipments of spent nuclear fuel and radioactive waste from other states. A Request for Information Response that Little signed and submitted to the federal government in March describes an accelerated process that takes “months rather than decades” to bring the “initial capabilities” of a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus online in 2027. But on Wednesday, Little said things aren’t moving that quickly. “There’s a long way to go before this happens,” Little said. “(The DOE) would love to identify some sites, and I believe … they may need something by the end of the year. But it will not be in any way, shape or form a final agreement.” Little said the documents he signed do not obligate Idaho to host an innovation campus or accept nuclear fuel or radioactive waste. Instead, the agreements simply bring Idaho to the negotiating table, the governor said. Little said it makes sense for Idaho to be at the negotiating table because of the potential economic benefits to the state, the infrastructure, the experience at Idaho National Laboratory in eastern Idaho and the need for additional, reliable energy. The memorandum of understanding lists a Sept. 30 deadline, but Little said he doesn’t think agreements will be reached that quickly, and he suggested the two sides could either continue talks or sign another memorandum of understanding with a later deadline. Officials at Idaho National Laboratory declined to comment for this series of articles. What is a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus? items.body: West Ada Education Services Director David Reinhart couldn’t get through a presentation to some 150 parents, teachers and community members without being shouted at Tuesday night. Interruptions from the crowd were occasionally met with applause or boos. Emotions were high: In November, district leaders will decide whether to close the district’s McMillan Elementary. Tuesday’s meeting was held to inform families and invite input. Reinhart persisted through the interruptions, sharing numbers through a projector above his head in the school’s gymnasium. It was the second such meeting at the school, but drew about 100 more attendees. The first meeting, on Sept. 16, drew about 50 people, KTVB reported. A school is more than just numbers, Reinhart said. But McMillan Elementary’s enrollment is shrinking, with nearly 300 empty seats. It needs around $5.5 million in repairs. Declining enrollment and pricey repair bills have led West Ada trustees to consider closing the school. Parents and teachers like the school. Class sizes hover around 19 students. Teachers say they know students by name and often remember them long after they move on to middle school. Still, declining enrollment prompted West Ada administrators to ask trustees to take a scrutinizing look at the school’s future. “T he decline in enrollment has been sharp, so we want to make good use of our resources, and that’s why we brought it to their attention,” Reinhart told parents. items.body: The Boise School District says it could close a number of schools, convert others, and revamp which grades attend high school and junior high as it faces declining enrollment. The district rolled out a number of proposals during virtual and in-person meetings this week it called “The Future of Boise Schools.” Meeting invitations didn’t hint at the scale of the proposed changes, but did note that final decisions have not been made. The proposals include shutting down or combining some grade schools, closing several junior high schools, moving high schools from three years to four, and possibly adding a specialized new high school. Declining enrollment Tracy Richter, a consultant, works with school districts across the country, which all face the same issue. “We don’t have a district that we’re working with anywhere in the country that is rising in enrollment,” Richter said, which he attributed to a decline in birth rates across the country. Factors like housing availability are also affecting school district enrollment — families may be holding onto homes longer, even after children have grown up and moved out, and young families may struggle to afford the homes that are available. When costs are prohibitive for young families to move in, it does not lead to more students for the district, Richter said. The housing market, Richter said, creates another barrier for families looking to move. “Nobody wants to go to half the house for twice the money and four times the interest rate.” Richter works for HPM, a consulting company contracted by the Boise School District to create a Long-Range Facilities Master Plan. The Boise School District currently has 9,000 open seats, 5,000 of which are at the elementary school level. Part of the plan aims to propose solutions to declining student enrollment, which is creating excess capacity, particularly at the district’s elementary and junior high schools. To do so, HPM has developed and is seeking public feedback on three potential scenarios: addressing excess capacity at the high school level, junior high level, or elementary school level. The company also developed “concepts,” or ways to implement each scenario, including closing some elementary schools in the district, moving 9th grade from the junior high to high school level, and changing enrollment areas and boundaries for schools. Richter presented each of the scenarios at a virtual and in-person meetings this week. District patrons are being encouraged to review the potential scenarios and concepts and submit their feedback via a Fall Community Survey , available on the district’s master planning webpage . Richter said that his team received 900 responses from an initial survey in the spring, which helped them develop the scenarios under consideration now. Richter anticipated it would take until February or March to develop a facilities master plan and make a recommendation that the district’s board of trustees would then adopt. “What we want people to understand is that we’re not even close to any recommendations yet,” Richter said, “and we want to make sure that we are doing as transparent of a process as we can to make sure we’re getting as much input as we can from the community.” The district could make decisions on any potential funding needed to implement the changes, such as bonds, after the master plan is established, Richter said. He estimated it could take two to five years for the district to implement any recommendation. items.body: Two Idaho colleges landed notable spots in U.S. News & World Report’s latest annual college rankings . The University of Idaho received a lofty national ranking for affordability, while a Moscow-based college — connected to a controversial church with ties to Christian nationalism — is Idaho’s highest-ranked liberal arts college. College and university leaders closely watch the annual rankings — and on Tuesday, the U of I and Lewis-Clark State College were quick to send out news releases touting their numbers. U.S. News & World Report uses more than 15 metrics for its overall college and university rankings. Student outcomes — graduation and retention rates and post-graduation earnings — account for 52% of the overall score. The magazine then sorts colleges and universities into several separate classifications. Here are some takeaways (with links to the full reports for each school): University of Idaho The U of I received the state’s top grade in the national universities category, receiving a middle-of-the-pack No. 208 ranking. U.S. News & World Report ranked 427 national universities. The U of I ranked highest on the list of “best value schools,” coming in No. 23 overall. The U of I is the highest-ranked public university in this category. For the past several years, the U of I has trailed only one other public institution, the University of North Carolina. “This ranking reflects what we work hard to deliver every day: an exceptional education that remains within reach for students and families,” U of I President Scott Green said in a news release. “Our students pursue research, learn by doing and build connections that prepare them to succeed after graduation, creating value not just for Idaho but nationally as well through the work they go on to do.” The U of I also ranked No. 66 as a best value school for in-state students. Boise State University Boise State ranked No. 299 in the national universities category. Its top-ranked program, nursing, came in at No. 94. Idaho State University Idaho State landed between No. 382 and No. 422 among national universities (no specific ranking was released). Idaho State’s highest-ranked program, also in nursing, came in at No. 135. Lewis-Clark State College LC State ranked No. 27 among 73 regional colleges in the West. LC State was also ranked No. 6 among public schools, climbing two spots from last year. The college also landed No. 23 for social mobility — which measures success rates for Pell Grant recipients — and climbed 12 spots in this category. In a news release, LC State noted that it is the only Top 10 public college in Idaho or Washington. “LC State continues to enhance the incredible value it provides to students, families, communities, and Idaho, and we’re grateful that this ranking captures that progression,” President Cynthia Pemberton said. Northwest Nazarene University NNU ranked No. 41 among 110 regional universities in the West. It ranked No. 19 among private schools, and No. 71 for social mobility. New Saint Andrews College New Saint Andrews ranked No. 132 among 206 national liberal arts colleges, and No. 121 among private schools. Doug Wilson — pastor of Moscow-based Christ Church — founded New Saint Andrews in 1994 and is a permanent member of the college’s board. (Click here for a 2024 Boise State Public Radio podcast series on Christian nationalism, with segments focused on Christ Church and Wilson.) The College of Idaho C of I ranked No. 142 among national liberal arts colleges, and No. 128 among private schools. Brigham Young University-Idaho BYU-Idaho, owned by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, ranked No. 172 among national liberal arts colleges, and No. 148 among private schools. Its undergraduate engineering program ranked No. 71.

items.body: CALDWELL — It was a refreshing night on the campaign trail Tuesday. And that’s exactly the problem. It’s unusual — make that rare — to see two statewide candidates on the same stage. Facing a live audience of voters. Answering actual questions. Talking in detail about priorities and policies. Two candidates, to their credit, taking their case to the people. I wish I could say Tuesday night’s debate between GOP state superintendent Debbie Critchfield and Democratic challenger Becky Sundin Mitchell was just the start of a robust fall debate season. That, unfortunately, wouldn’t be honest. See for yourself. Click here to watch Tuesday’s debate. The fact is that Tuesday’s debate — co-sponsored by Idaho EdNews and The College of Idaho — is the exception to the rule. Critchfield and Sundin Mitchell will appear again at an Oct. 12 debate sponsored by KTVB in Boise. Aside from that, it’s quiet out there. Way too quiet. Other Republican incumbents aren’t debating. Gov. Brad Little, Sen. Jim Risch and Attorney General Raúl Labrador either turned down or ignored invites from KTVB. What gives? In the spirit of the election season — and the spirit of helping you make an informed choice — pick your favorite sports metaphor. Marc Johnson, a longtime fixture in former Gov. Cecil Andrus’ inner circle, recently invoked the name of legendary North Carolina basketball coach Dean Smith. Johnson — who seldom passes up the chance to chide Idaho Republicans in general, and Risch in particular — accused Idaho’s junior senator of cribbing Smith’s “four-corners” offense . When Smith’s teams had what appeared to be an insurmountable lead, he’d spread players on the four corners of the front court, directing them to pass the ball around with no intention of taking a shot or doing, well, anything. An annoying but maddeningly effective way to run out the clock. Not to try to upstage Johnson, I’ll call the no-debate gameplan a “business decision.” In football, when a player sidesteps a hit from an opposing player, usually a bigger one moving at full speed, that’s a business decision. Avoid a potential injury — or, at least, some short-term pain — and protect your future earnings potential. Call bailing on debates whatever you want. Just don’t call it gutsy. And their opponents, standing on the sidelines, have little left to do but grumble. At a town hall meeting in Boise last week, independent gubernatorial candidate John Stegner was asked whether he’d get the chance at a debate. He said he wasn’t counting on it. “(It’s) disconcerting at best (and) disheartening at worst,” said Stegner, picking his words with the deliberation befitting a former state Supreme Court justice. Independent Senate candidate Todd Achilles got some social media traffic and some news coverage recently, by recording a brief and awkward Boise Airport exchange with Risch . Achilles tried to get Risch to commit to a debate. Risch walked away; at the end of the video, Risch is seen talking to airport security. Achilles tried to keep the narrative going in a campaign text a few days later. “Todd again,” the text began. “Risch still has not said a word since he pulled his hand away and kept walking.” Democratic challenger Becky Sundin Mitchell, right, and Republican incumbent Debbie Critchfield participate in a debate for Idaho Superintendent of Public Instruction on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026, at the College of Idaho in Caldwell. items.body: Charles Fain, who in 2001 was exonerated and freed from prison after 16 years, speaks at a Sept. 17, 2026, event in Boise to announce a new nonprofit taking up the work of trying to overturn wrongful convictions in the state. To his right are retired founder of the Idaho Innocence Project Greg Hampikian and The Innocence Center Executive Director Mike Semanchik. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Correction: This story was corrected at 2:08 p.m. on Sept. 24 to clarify the Idaho Innocence Project’s role in Charles Fain’s case. The Idaho Innocence Project helped secure Fain’s certificate of innocence and identify the true perpetrator, but was not involved in his original exoneration. Charles Fain says his three favorite letters in the alphabet are D-N-A. In 2001, Fain was exonerated and released from an Idaho prison after nearly 20 years on death row for a rape and murder he did not commit, using DNA analysis. After his release, the Idaho Innocence Project helped police identify the true perpetrator and got Fain a certificate of innocence and compensation for wrongful conviction. The Idaho Innocence Project has been shuttered for more than two years because of a lack of funding. However, on Sept. 17, Fain joined Innocence Project founder Greg Hampikian and fellow exoneree Amanda Knox to usher in a new group continuing the work of overturning wrongful convictions. The Innocence Center board member and exoneree Amanda Knox and retired founder of the Idaho Innocence Project Greg Hampikian. Hampikian lent his DNA expertise to Knox’s defense team to help free her from an Italian prison. (Photo by G Kenny3 Photography) Knox sits on the board of The Innocence Center , a nonprofit, free law firm based in San Diego that will take on cases in Idaho to try and free wrongfully convicted inmates. Hampikian, a forensic DNA expert, also lent his expertise to Knox’s defense team in the highly publicized case and helped free her from an Italian prison after she was wrongfully sentenced for the murder of her roommate while studying abroad. “It would be a desperate situation if these projects didn’t exist,” Knox said in an interview last week in Boise. “And when I heard that the Idaho Innocence Project was shutting down, I was really, really worried for the state of Idaho, because who else is going to do it?” The Innocence Center Executive Director Mike Semanchik was admitted to the Idaho bar on Sept. 18 so that he may work as an attorney for these cases in Idaho. “We’re committed to making this happen and making sure that wherever there are innocent people in prison, there’s an organization to support them,” Semanchik told a small gathering last week to kickoff the new work. Hampikian said he personally selected The Innocence Center to take up the work. “My last great act, after 20 years of the Innocence Project, was to choose a successor,” Hampikian said. “… (Semanchik) said, ‘I’ll get barred in Idaho, and I’ll take the cases until we raise the money.’ And I was like, ‘Oh, this guy’s got skin in the game.’” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. The Idaho Rural Health Transformation Program Im
items.body: The Idaho Rural Health Transformation Program Implementation Task Force meets on Sept. 23, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) A group of rural Idaho hospital leaders, state officials and tribal representatives met for the first time Wednesday to oversee the process of awarding nearly $190 million in federal rural health grants. The Idaho Rural Health Transformation Program Implementation Task Force received an update on the state’s administration of the federal Rural Health Transformation grant program — a nationwide $50 billion, five-year federal grant Congress approved through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year. Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare) “We are building and flying the plane at the same time. That feels like it’s been the consistent theme of this,” Idaho Department Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron said Wednesday. The task force is meant to provide input on the process of implementation, help navigate potential challenges, and ensure the state is balancing statewide initiatives with actual needs of rural communities, Charron said. The nearly 20 funding opportunities posted by the state have closed, and Health and Welfare staff are reviewing applications to award subgrants. The opportunities include funding to provide school-based family support, chronic disease prevention and cancer screening, a cognitive care network, and diabetes prevention and management. The agency awarded national nonprofit Comagine Health with a grant to create a collaborative system to improve maternal and child health statewide, according to the program website. The state is nearing an Oct. 30 deadline to award all of the $186 million received for the first year of the program. “It is going to be a very, very tight timeline coming up to the end,” Charron said. For a health provider infrastructure opportunity, which will be about $97 million of the total grant, Charron said the agency received more than 250 applications asking for a total of more than $300 million. “That means that we will have to say no to some,” she said. Idaho submitted its first required report to the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid, which is overseeing the program, on Aug. 31. The report will help determine how much funding the state gets in the second year of the five-year program. Charron said that the state hasn’t heard feedback on that report yet. SUBSCRIBE Idaho’s received sightly less funding because of low rural population density When Congress approved the funding, it split the $50 billion into two allocation methods. Half of the money was split equally among all 50 states. The remaining $25 billion was to be distributed based on certain metrics. Idaho’s low population density in rural communities and low density of rural healthcare providers were “challenges” for the scoring criteria, Charron said “Centers for Medicare and Medicaid had very specific criteria to drill down into: What does rural healthcare delivery look like in that specific state? And this is where we were a bit challenged, frankly, because we are so frontier in our state,” she said. (Photo by Hayat Norimine/KFF Health News) This story was first published by KFF Health News on Sept. 22, 2026. Joshua and Ashley Durham run a family medicine practice, and for the first time in their lives, they have no health insurance. When the Durhams began their practice at the end of 2023 — he as a primary care physician and she as a pharmacist who handles the billing — the couple bought coverage for themselves and their two kids on the Affordable Care Act marketplace. But they said their monthly premiums for a similar health plan for this year rose several hundred dollars to nearly $1,600. Top insurance official recommends task force for studying Idaho’s most critical healthcare issues They decided to pay out-of-pocket for their medical expenses instead, leaning on $50,000 they had set aside in a health savings account over several years. “It’s nerve-racking,” said Joshua Durham, 47. “It just takes, you know, one little accident, and then you got a big fat bill.” The healthcare industry traditionally has more of its workforce on medical insurance than many other fields. Nationwide, 7% of all healthcare workers were uninsured in 2024, compared with 11% of all adults under 65, according to a KFF analysis of the most recent American Community Survey data. And doctors were especially unlikely to forgo health insurance, with just 2% uninsured. But even healthcare workers are feeling the pinch as health insurance costs rise each year, with employers expecting that costs will jump an additional 8.2% for 2027. The Republican-led Congress also opted last year not to renew Affordable Care Act marketplace credits enacted during the covid pandemic. While subsidies remain in place for people with low incomes, the pandemic-era credits helped reduce many consumers’ premium payments , especially those working in small businesses such as independent medical practices. Nearly half of marketplace enrollees worked for small businesses or were self-employed in 2024; some of the most common occupations included chiropractic care and dentistry. Jack Dillon, executive director of the Association for Independent Medicine , which represents 4,000 physician-led practices, said premium increases have become untenable for small businesses, whether employers seek coverage through the marketplace or directly from insurers. “The cost has become so astronomical,” Dillon said. “You’re looking at it and saying, ‘What’s the value?’” As health insurance continues to become less affordable, Dillon said, more healthcare employers may seek alternatives to their standard coverage, such as providing higher hourly wages or providing only minimal plans. items.body: School funding was central to both candidates’ pitches at Tuesday’s state superintendent debate at the College of Idaho. Republican incumbent Debbie Critchfield touted her efforts this spring and summer to rewrite the state’s more than 30-year-old funding formula, her top priority if re-elected. She pointed to her relationships with legislators as key to passing a fund for high-needs students last legislative session, along with other education priorities. Those relationships, she said, will help her push a funding formula rewrite across the finish line next session if reelected. Democratic challenger Becky Sundin Mitchell emphasized enrollment-based funding and questioned whether Critchfield could succeed where previous state superintendents failed: getting lawmakers to approve a new K-12 funding formula. Sundin Mitchell stressed that Idaho’s public schools need more funds, in general, as they routinely rank 51st in the nation for per-pupil spending . She repeatedly called for legislators to spend more time in public schools. The debate, hosted by Idaho Education News and The College of Idaho, provided a glimpse into the candidates’ different approaches to school funding and a range of other issues, including the state superintendent’s role, a lingering special education funding gap, Idaho’s new private school tax credit law, and how much politics should shape education policy. items.body: The Ninth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals as photographed on June 12, 2017, in San Francisco, California. A panel of Ninth Circuit judges heard arguments Tuesday in a lawsuit challenging Idaho's abortion ban, seeking expanded exemptions. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) A panel of federal appeals judges will soon decide whether to continue to allow full enforcement of Idaho’s abortion bans, or to allow a lower court’s previous ruling that provided more exemptions to the law. U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit Judges Kim McLane Wardlaw, Marsha Berzon and Consuelo Callahan heard oral arguments in a virtual hearing Tuesday afternoon. The state of Idaho, represented by an attorney from the conservative Christian legal advocacy group Alliance Defending Freedom , argued that the laws should be fully enforced as written. Idaho’s laws prohibit most abortions, except in cases to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors face felony penalties and civil lawsuits of a minimum of $20,000 if they perform the procedure outside those exemptions. ADF attorney Mathew Hoffmann argued that a lower court’s previous ruling that would’ve expanded exemptions to apply to serious health and mental health risks to the mother, was not grounded in historical precedent. He said there is no right to “therapeutic” abortions. Attorneys representing Boise maternal-fetal medicine specialist Dr. Stacy Seyb argued that an earlier court decision from U.S. District of Idaho Judge B. Lynn Winmill should go back into effect. The ruling would’ve prevented the Ada County prosecutor and Idaho attorney general from enforcing Idaho’s abortion ban in cases where the mother’s health faced serious risk or her life was at risk due to self harm. Winmill later narrowed this block on enforcement to only protect abortions performed by Seyb. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador. (Photo courtesy of Attorney General Raúl Labrador) After Attorney General Raúl Labrador appealed, a Ninth Circuit panel placed a hold on Winmill’s order, and the law went back into effect. Hoffmann said Winmill’s decision expanding the exemptions created “an abortion-on-demand regime.” “They leave it up to the subjective judgment of doctors to determine a risk sufficient to justify abortion,” he said. Stephanie Toti, executive director of the Lawyering Project, argued on behalf of Seyb that the expanded exemptions to the law were necessary. “The injunction entered by the district court in this case is narrow. It would enable only a small number of patients each year to obtain an abortion,” Toti said. “But for those patients, access to that care is vitally important, as the district court found.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. Wade and sent regulation of abortion to the states, would allow a court to expand a state’s exemptions. Hoffmann argued that it would not, because the Constitution does not explicitly provide a right to abortions. Toti argued that the 2022 decision did not mention rights to life and health, which she said are violated by the Idaho ban’s limited exemptions. Callahan questioned Toti over whether the request to allow abortions for serious risk of self harm was “weaker” than the other arguments. “We have a right to life, but you don’t have a right to kill yourself, right?” Callahan asked. Toti responded that patients seeking an abortion to prevent death by self-harm, “don’t want to kill themselves.” “They want to remain alive. items.body: The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State's Office, the University of Idaho's College of Law and Boise State University's Institute for Advancing American Values. (Photo by Getty Images) A new gathering aims to bring together policymakers, students and the public to discuss the U.S. Constitution’s protections for free speech and encourage civil discourse. The inaugural Idaho Free Speech Summit will take place on Oct. 13 in Boise through the partnership of the Secretary of State’s Office, the University of Idaho’s College of Law and Boise State University’s Institute for Advancing American Values , according to a Secretary of State’s Office press release. The keynote speaker for the event will be Utah Gov. Spencer Cox, who has championed Disagree Better, a national, nonpartisan initiative “designed to reduce inflammatory rhetoric and foster a culture of healthy debate,” according to its website. Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. (Photo courtesy of Phil McGrane) “Free speech is fundamental to our system of government, but protecting it requires more than simply agreeing that it is important,” said Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane. “It means listening to people we disagree with, defending their right to speak, and being willing to have difficult conversations. That is what we hope to accomplish with the Idaho Free Speech Summit.” Sessions at the summit will explore First Amendment issues “ranging from campaign finance and campus free speech to the broader challenges of maintaining civil discourse in an increasingly divided political environment,” the press release said. Lt. Gov. Deidre Henderson (left) listens as Gov. Spencer Cox holds a press conference to present his budget proposal at the Salt Lake County Library in Kearns, Utah, on Dec. 3, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) Cox will talk about how Americans can disagree without abandoning strongly held beliefs, a theme he explores in his new book, “Off Ramp: How to Be a Peacemaker in an Age of Contempt,” according to the release. “We are pleased to be part of a discussion centered on one of our nation’s most important constitutional freedoms,” said Brian Kane, University of Idaho College of Law dean, in the release. “The University of Idaho College of Law is a natural partner for this conversation. Law schools should be places where difficult constitutional questions are examined carefully and where people learn how to engage seriously with ideas they may not share.” The daylong summit will have presentations and panel discussions, followed by an evening reception. A continuing legal education credit will also be available for participating attorneys. “Universities have an important role to play in creating spaces where people can wrestle with difficult questions and hear perspectives different from their own,” said Boise State University’s Andrew Finstuen in the release. “The Summit provides an opportunity to model the kind of thoughtful, constructive dialogue that is essential to a healthy civic culture.” Registration and additional information, including the Summit schedule and speaker lineup, are available at FreeSpeechIdaho.com . “Our goal isn’t to bring together people who all agree,” McGrane said in the release. “It is to bring together people who recognize that our constitutional freedoms are strongest when we defend the right of others to speak, listen to one another, and engage in good faith.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: A $7.9 million lab expansion is slated to begin this fall at Idaho State University’s Meridian campus — a project geared to support two partners seeking to address Idaho’s physician shortage. The project will add a 16-station human anatomy lab and a two-station embalming suite at the L.S. and Aline W. Skaggs Treasure Valley Anatomy and Physiology Laboratories. The building is home to a 34-station anatomy lab, Idaho State said in a news release. But demand is increasing, and the 6,130-square-foot remodel is designed to keep up with future growth. “We have a decade of very successful operations under our belt,” said Padma Gadepally, director of anatomy laboratories and clinical assistant professor at Idaho State. “We started with about 50 learners and now have upwards of 2,000 learners.” Existing lab space at the L.S. and Aline W. Skaggs Treasure Valley Anatomy and Physiology Laboratories. And in 2025, the adjacent Idaho College of Osteopathic Medicine increased enrollment by 75 students per cohort, increasing the need for the remodel. ICOM is the state’s sole medical school. “This project reflects our shared commitment to educating the next generation of healthcare professionals and ensuring Idaho communities have access to highly trained providers for years to come,” ICOM chair of anatomy Blaine Maley said in the Idaho State release. The expansion will also support another piece of Idaho’s medical education puzzle: a partnership between the University of Idaho and the University of Utah. The two universities are working on a medical education program at the U of I’s Boise campus, and their students would be able to use Idaho State’s new facilities. “This is the kind of partnership Idaho needs to grow its own healthcare workforce,” Rayme Geidl, co-director of the U of I School of Health and Medical Professions, said in the Idaho State release. “Collaborations like this show what’s possible when Idaho institutions work together.”

items.body: Sal Soto struggled through high school, making it to graduation with the help of summer classes. He never thought decades later he’d be back at high school every day as a teacher, helping students like himself. Soto, 44, is the culinary teacher at Elevate Academy Nampa, one of a handful of career technical education charter schools in the Elevate network statewide. At Elevate, he has turned his experience as a restaurant owner into more than a culinary program. His classroom is built around relationships, hands-on learning, and the idea that students can learn from their mistakes — lessons Soto says he learned the hard way. Learning the family business Soto was born and raised in Caldwell. His parents immigrated from Mexico and worked their way up at major Idaho agribusiness company JR Simplot Co. When he was 12, the Sotos took a risk opening Imelda’s, a TexMex restaurant in Caldwell. His mother, Imelda, used family recipes to create the restaurant’s menu. “It was a lot of stress on them,” Soto said. “She would be like, ‘Was this a good switch’ from being a boss at Simplot to opening up her own business.” Soto would do his homework at the restaurant before helping wherever he was needed. He graduated high school and did odd jobs for a few years before being drawn back to the restaurant, which he purchased from his mother in his early 20s. His mother taught him how to cook. “I had many fails,” Soto said with a chuckle. He was nervous taking over the business and trying to prove himself to the customers. “We got really busy,” he said. “It was stressful. It was like, ‘OK this is a lot on me.'” The regular customers were the best part, Soto said. The restaurant is near the College of Idaho campus, so basketball, football and volleyball players would come frequently. It began to feel like family. (Sean Dolan/EdNews) Cultivating a career change Soto ran the restaurant for 20 years. When Imelda retired, Soto and his wife questioned what their next step would be. The couple had young daughters, and Soto was missing much of family life. “I would get there at five in the morning, and sometimes I wouldn’t get home until eight, nine o’clock,” he said. He sold the business for a better work-life balance. Not long after, his cousin, Esai Longoria, who works at Elevate Caldwell, suggested Soto apply to teach at the new campus in Nampa. He got the job — and faced a massive learning curve. “I’ve never taught before, so I didn’t know what to do,” he said. “That first year was a struggle. I just wanted to make sure I did the job right.” He earned a teaching certificate at the College of Idaho, built a curriculum and worked with other Elevate staff. items.body: Absentee ballots are prepared to be mailed at the Wake County Board of Elections on September 17, 2024 in Raleigh, North Carolina. (Photo by Allison Joyce/Getty Images) With less than two months before the 2026 midterm elections, election officials across Idaho mailed the first round of mail-in ballots to voters who are overseas or who requested absentee ballots locally. The finalization of ballots in Idaho follows after a weekslong crunch to change contested language for an abortion legalization ballot initiative and attempts by the Trump administration to implement a federal rule that could’ve made last-minute changes to ballots. Idaho election officials worry about mail-in ballot changes proposed by Trump administration “Everything is on track,” said Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, the state’s top election official who’s running for re-election as a Republican. More than a month before the Nov. 3 general election, local election officials are expected to finalize ballots. That’s because federal law requires the first slate of mail-in ballots be shipped 45 days before federal elections to voters who are overseas, such as members of the military or missionaries. In Ada County, Idaho’s largest, election officials were expecting to mail out more than 24,000 ballots on Friday, Trent Tripple, the Republican county clerk, told the Idaho Capital Sun. That includes overseas and military voters, along with everyone who had already requested an absentee ballot, he said. Voters still have more than a month to request absentee ballots or register to vote before Election Day. Oct. 23 is the deadline to request absentee ballots or pre-register to vote, according to an election calendar on VoteIdaho.gov , a website run by the Secretary of State’s Office. This year, all statewide constitutional offices — such as governor, lieutenant governor, and attorney general — are up for election as well as all 105 seats in the Idaho Legislature. Three of Idaho’s four congressional seats will also be on the ballot. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE The crunch to finalize ballots in Idaho Election officials in Ada County — which is home to Boise — had told the state they were working on a Sept. 9 deadline to finalize the design of ballots ahead of shipping the first round of absentee ballots out. Idaho Secretary of State candidate Phil McGrane talks with a supporter during the Idaho Republican Party primary celebration on May 17, 2022. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) One legal dispute came close to that deadline. With just four days left to go until Ada County’s deadline, the Idaho Supreme Court quickly finished its work resolving a lawsuit by the organizers of the abortion ballot initiative. On the Friday before Labor Day weekend, the state’s high court required state officials, including McGrane, to rewrite statements about what votes on the initiative would do. Before the work week started, the court had approved redrafted language. “It could’ve gotten a lot closer to the wire,” McGrane said in an interview. “It is impressive that the Idaho Supreme Court was issuing decisions on Sunday during Labor Day weekend in an effort to meet the deadline.” Making changes to ballot design close to the deadline is more than changing a single ballot, election officials say. items.body: The Columbia Princess Ferry stays on the Gifford side of the Columbia River as the Modrite Fire exhibits extreme fire behavior just south of Inchelium, Washington. Fires in the state hit tribes particularly hard this year. (Photo courtesy of Colville Tribal Broadcasts, News and Information) Neighbors across the Colville Tribes communities in Washington state knew Matilda Bob’s log home as the “rainbow house,” for its brightly painted exterior. Now it’s gone. Sparked by a lightning strike in mid-July, the Kaiser Canyon Fire destroyed Bob’s home and 42 other houses on the Colville Reservation, along with 100 outbuildings such as sheds and barns, tribal leaders said. “I couldn’t believe that it had happened,” said Bob. “It went so fast.” Tribal leaders across Washington and Oregon told Stateline that this year’s record-breaking wildfires burned timber that they rely on for income, threatened food sources and waterways, and harmed the health of their communities. Power outages left families without food they’ve hunted or gathered and frozen. Hotter, drier conditions driven by climate change already have made wildfires nationwide more frequent and intense, a trend that is expected to accelerate. Substandard housing and higher rates of acute and chronic underlying health conditions, including respiratory illnesses, make tribal communities more vulnerable during and after the fires. “What typically used to be like a two-month fire season for us when I first started fighting fire about 25 years ago — now that’s at least three months and sometimes longer, depending on the year,” said Cody Desautel , executive director of the Colville Tribes, who is also a forester and wildland fire expert. An especially warm winter also left Washington state with about half its usual snowpack, raising drought concerns and wildfire risks. Nighttime view of the Kaiser Canyon Fire during firing operations on Whitmore Mountain. (Photo courtesy of Colville Tribal Broadcasts, News and Information) This year saw particularly devastating fires in eastern Washington, including arson-instigated fires that destroyed over 700 homes in Spokane. The conditions prompted Washington state Democratic Gov. Bob Ferguson to declare a statewide state of emergency on Aug. 1, citing an “unprecedented” red flag alert of extreme fire danger from the National Weather Service. The Colville Reservation includes the southern portion of Ferry County, which has the second-lowest median household income of all counties in the state. The tribe lost a significant amount of timber, a main source of income, during the fires. (Photo by Getty Images) Here’s something that you should not pass up. The Kuna Lions (my club) is sponsoring health screening for vision, hearing and diabetes from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Oct. 10 at Kuna’s community center. The vision and hearing screening will be conducted by Envision , and Terry Reilly Health Services will be doing the diabetes testing. People living in surrounding communities are cordially invited. If there were a poster boy for diabetes screening, it would be me. This has been a summer of amputations – one toe on my right foot and two partial toe amputations on my left foot. I have not been able to do summer activities that I enjoy, such as daily walks around the neighborhood and golf. Yes, these amputations were the result of diabetes. On the bright side, losing a couple of toes is a lot better than losing a foot or a leg. But there’s more to my diabetes story. Twenty-two years ago, I had a five-way heart bypass surgery – which has given me more than two decades of quality living. But veins from that surgery don’t last forever, and some of mine have shown signs of wear. In football terms, I may be getting close to the two minute warning. But as fans know so well, a lot can happen in those last two minutes. I have a great life, and it isn’t done yet. I might have been spared from some of these health challenges if I had diabetes screening 30 years ago. Instead, I ignored some of the obvious symptoms. Recently, I had a chat with Dr. Stuart Black with Terry Reilly Health Services, and he knows all about the importance of the screening. “Some studies show that 10 percent of the population, and as high as 13 percent have diabetes and maybe a fourth of the people with diabetes don’t know about it,” he said. “If screening shows an indication of prediabetes, people can get the care they need and prevent the complications that come with the disease, such as heart disease and kidney problems. Diabetes also is one of the leading causes for blindness.” Dr. Black says that random glucose readings at a screening event may not paint the true picture. For instance, numbers may be on the high side for those who had something to eat before the screening. But high numbers are worth watching. “The more information that a person has, the better,” he says. “I think there are people who are afraid to find out they have diabetes, because they think it’s a death sentence. But that’s not the case. There are great options to help control blood sugars if you have diabetes or prediabetes.” Terry Reilly’s service doesn’t stop with the screening. It’s also a resource, and a relatively affordable one, for those who show signs of prediabetes or diabetes. Terry Reilly Health Services, based in Nampa, has other area clinics – including one in Melba. “We have physicians and clinical pharmacists who are well versed in dealing with diabetes,” Dr. Black said. “Our doors are open to help anyone who is diagnosed, or at risk, for diabetes or prediabetes.” Of course, he says, there are steps people can take without a doctor’s help. “Getting 150 minutes of exercise in a week; eating a healthy diet that focuses more on fruits, vegetables and less on fast foods or processed foods; getting enough sleep; decreasing stress in your life,” he said. “All those things are basic lifestyle choices that people can take, with or without diabetes.” I wish I had followed that advice 30 years ago. items.body: The Canyon County Sheriff’s Office on Friday confirmed its investigation into the Vallivue School District’s 2024 land deal is still active. Idaho EdNews broke the story on April 17. “No updates at this time, investigation still active,” a detective with the criminal investigation division told EdNews Friday. The district in 2024 bought 87 acres of farmland from Dave Christensen, the father of trustee Clay Christensen, for $5 million. The land, intended for the site of a school, was appraised at $2.87 million. “I knew about what I wanted, and, you know, it was really the only way I probably would have sold it,” Dave Christensen told EdNews in April about his $5 million price tag for the land. Idaho code requires trustees to have property appraised before a purchase and that appraisal “shall be used to establish the value of the real property.” Superintendent Lisa Boyd at the time defended the purchase and said the district complied with statute. Later that month, EdNews obtained records from several other Idaho school districts that showed Vallivue’s deal bucked the norm by millions. Five different land purchases in districts from around the state came in under the appraised value — and in two deals landowners gifted chunks of property — according to public records EdNews examined in a spot check of transactions over the past two decades. Vallivue trustees have declined to answer any questions about the land deal. Trustee Toni Brinegar, who was board chair at the time of the 2024 purchase, referred EdNews to their attorney. Two trustees have since resigned, leaving the board with three members. Brinegar resigned in June, and Paul Tierney resigned in August. Boyd said both trustees had planned to resign after their kids graduated from Vallivue schools. The district is looking for interested residents to apply for the vacancies.

Sara LaWall, the minister for the Boise Unitarian Universalist Fellowship, and eight others who were protesting bills restricting transgender rights were arrested this spring after refusing to leave the lobby to the office of Idaho Gov. Brad Little, whom the protestors said they were hoping to meet with. LaWall’s defense attorney cast her actions during the protest as an act of civil disobedience, an act that involves intentionally breaking laws for moral reasons. In a statement before the judge delivered his sentence, LaWall, who has a transgender daughter, said she had repeatedly attempted to relay her concerns over anti-trans bills with elected officials. “We followed every available path of redress (grievenances) within our system. Our fears and concerns, and frankly, our begging and pleading, went unheard and unanswered,” LaWall said, citing legislators cutting off testimony early on an anti-trans bill where doctors planned to testify. She said she understands her actions have consequences, and she said she accepts full responsibility for her actions. “I do not take this lightly,” LaWall said. “I knew the risks when I chose to stay. But I was willing then and am willing now to accept the risks as an act of faithful witness and solidarity with my daughter, all the beautiful trans youth, and the incredible trans community here in Idaho. Many of whom I am blessed to call my friends and chosen family — all of whom must negotiate risk and their own safety every day, just by being who they are.” Before issuing the sentence, Idaho 4th District Judge Adam Kimball said he was weighing several factors — such as protecting society and deterring LaWall and others from violating the law. But he said he didn’t find probation necessary in this case. “It’s my hope that you will be heard the way you wish, and that if you are not, that you do not break the law to be heard. (Photo by Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The Constitution Party candidate in Idaho’s 1st Congressional District election has pleaded guilty to possessing “child sexually exploitative material.” He is still eligible for office under the U.S. Constitution. Brendan Gomez, 27, was arrested in early July by Ada County Sheriff’s Office detectives at a home in Boise, Channel 2 Idaho News reported. He was booked into the Ada County jail and held on $500,000 bail, according to the jail roster. He was charged with 10 counts of willfully possessing child sex abuse material, according to state court records. He entered a plea deal Monday, pleading guilty to two counts of possession of sexually exploitative materials. His sentencing hearing is scheduled for Nov. 16, according to court records. The state recommended Gomez serve a fixed term of three years in prison, with 12 years indeterminate. Gomez’s attorney could not be immediately reached for this story. Gomez also ran for Congress in 2024, earning about 1.5% of the vote in the general election. In 2022, he ran unsuccessfully against incumbent state Sen. Lori Den Hartog to represent District 22 in the Idaho Legislature. Gomez’s name will still appear on the ballot for the Nov. 3 general election. He is running against incumbent Republican U.S. House Rep. Russ Fulcher, Democrat Kaylee Peterson, and independent Sarah Zabel. The deadline to withdraw from the ballot was Sept. 4. Under the Idaho Constitution , convicted felons are ineligible for state or local office until they fulfill their sentence, but there are no such restrictions for federal elected officials. Members of the U.S. House must be at least 25 years old, a U.S. citizen for at least seven years, and an inhabitant of the state they represent.The U.S. Constitution does not otherwise limit eligibility. Under U.S. House rules , members who are convicted of a crime with a sentence of two or more years of imprisonment “should refrain” from participating in votes and “should resign” from any committee. But if graded on a curve, the Boise State and U of I grades look a little bit better. Both universities received a “D” from the Philadelphia-based Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression . Using student surveys, FIRE ranked 261 colleges and universities; 121 received failing grades. The September 2025 slaying of conservative activist Charlie Kirk had far-reaching effects, FIRE said. Some colleges denied recognition for chapters of Kirk’s Turning Point USA, while nine schools punished faculty members who publicly criticized Kirk. “The overall state of free speech on campus is grim,” FIRE President and CEO Greg Lukianoff said in a news release. “Too many college administrators wield their power to cancel controversial speakers, cave to government or student calls for censorship, and limit academic freedom.” FIRE rated only two Idaho universities. Click on the links for the full reports on Boise State and the U of I . Here are a few thumbnails. But the university ranked in the bottom 50 for “openness,” according to the FIRE report, “meaning many contentious topics feel off-limits to students.” Anonymous student quotes from FIRE’s survey One student reported an exchange from class: A professor said she was very upset with the outcome of the presidential election, and asked students to sum up their thoughts in one word. The student had a response in mind, contentment, but was reluctant to express it. “I thought I would get attacked or judged if I said that,” the student wrote. items.body: Here’s a not-so-bold prediction: It won’t take the State Board of Education a tortured 16 months to hire the next University of Idaho president. This next search almost has to go more smoothly than the last presidential search — the one that finally ended on July 1, when David Hahn took the reins at Boise State University . Smooth and transparent are two different things, however. And transparency is a thing of the past, due to a new state law that moves the presidential search process almost entirely out of public view. Retiring University of Idaho President C. Scott Green (U of I photo) " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/C.-Scott-Green-graduation-e1789667075837-1180x765.jpg" class="wp-image-125466 size-large" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/C.-Scott-Green-graduation-1180x787.jpg" alt="" width="1180" height="787" /> Retiring University of Idaho President C. Scott Green (U of I photo) So perhaps sometime next spring or thereabouts, the State Board will announce a successor to U of I President C. Scott Green , who announced his retirement last week. The vast majority of the Vandal family — students, parents, faculty and staff, alums and donors — will have only a vague idea of how the board reached its decision. They’ll never really know why the board made its pick, or who else wanted the job. In other words, expect lots of secrecy. What else can we expect this time around? Here are a few other predictions, based on the Boise State search. Expect a slower start . Actually, that’s happening already. In March 2025, Marlene Tromp put the State Board squarely on the clock. She abruptly accepted the University of Vermont presidency , in the middle of Boise State’s spring semester, with plans to leave at the end of the school year. The State Board announced its presidential search committee the day after Tromp accepted the Vermont job. The goal — perhaps unworkable from Day One — was to find Tromp’s replacement in time for the 2025-26 school year. Because Green is retiring, and not switching jobs, he is giving the State Board a lot longer runway. He will stay on at the U of I through June 30, the end of the academic year. That’s important, because college and university presidents often switch jobs in the summer. The State Board will be in no hurry to get the U of I job on the market for the summer hiring rush. At the front end, that gives the State Board a little more time to assemble a search committee and hire a search firm. It doesn’t mean the search will be more transparent. Just less pell-mell. The search committee could offer a big tipoff . The new law sets minimum requirements for the search committee: two State Board members, two university employees, two alumni, a foundation representative and a community representative. That’s all. (And no, students aren’t guaranteed a seat at the table.) There’s nothing stopping the State Board from naming more committee members. Or stacking an eight-member committee with a distinct emphasis. Regardless, watch the committee makeup. It matters, a lot. David Hahn, the sole finalist for the Boise State presidency, speaks to reporters in a Tuesday, June 16, 2026 press conference.
