items.body: Teachers and secondary students in the Nampa School District will get new MacBooks next year in a move to counter the rising cost of PCs as AI data companies gobble up the supply of computer parts. Nampa students have been using 11-inch HP Pro laptops that run on Windows, but trustees on Tuesday approved a four-year, $5.6 million lease agreement with Apple to switch to 13-inch MacBook Neos for students in grades 6-12. For years, Apple laptops have been more expensive than PCs. But Assistant Superintendent of Operations Cortney Stauffer told the school board that has changed. He said the switch to Apple will save an estimated $1.4 million over four years. Elementary students will continue to use iPads. Cortney Stauffer, executive director of operations for the Nampa School District " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-944x1180.jpg" class="wp-image-105832 size-thumbnail" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-160x200.jpg" alt="" width="160" height="200" srcset="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-160x200.jpg 160w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-496x620.jpg 496w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-944x1180.jpg 944w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108-1229x1536.jpg 1229w, https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/S0A0108.jpg 1536w" sizes="auto, (max-width: 160px) 100vw, 160px" /> Nampa Assistant Superintendent of Operations Cortney Stauffer “The PCs, believe it or not, are now significantly more expensive than an Apple Neo,” Stauffer said. Nampa’s switch to Apple comes months after the Boise School District made the same move. Boise trustees in July approved a five-year, $18 million lease agreement with Apple for 22,000 devices. “What we saw coming is a dramatic increase in prices,” Boise Director of People and Organization Services Will Goodman said. As EdNews reported in July , Idaho school districts face soaring PC prices as AI data centers buy up computer parts. Boise’s own Micron Technology, a large producer of computer memory and storage, announced in December that it made the “difficult decision” to exit the consumer market and sell only to AI companies to accommodate the “surge in demand” for data centers. Gordon Howard, director of technology for Bonneville School District, told EdNews that Micron’s exit is leading to higher costs for all sorts of technology. He said the cost of Chromebooks has increased by $100 over the past year, and the cost to buy new servers for the district increased from $6,000 to $10,000 within three months. “It’s not just Chromebooks,” Howard said. “It’s everything.” The resale value of Chromebooks is low compared to Apple products. Bonneville in July sold 1,488 Acer Chromebooks for $5 a piece. Howard said the district usually keeps Chromebooks for seven years, but that model of Acer Chromebooks became too expensive to maintain after just four years. Screens and keyboards were breaking. “It was just going to cost us too much to maintain them,” he said. “The breakthrough rate was just too high.” By switching to MacBooks, Nampa hopes to avoid that issue. The lease agreement includes 6,000 MacBook Neos for students and 650 MacBook Airs for teachers. At the end of the lease, the district will own the devices and can sell them back to Apple with a guaranteed buyback price of $120 for the Neos and $275 for the Airs. “This is actually a wonderful opportunity for the district,” Stauffer told trustees. Currently, students in Nampa are responsible for all damage to the PCs. Repair costs range from $50 to $120. Parents can purchase insurance for $25 a year to avoid those costs. items.body: Members of the Idaho Legislature's Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee and their staff tour Southwest Idaho Treatment Center, or SWITC, in Nampa on Nov. 20, 2024. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun) In January, as Idaho state lawmakers prepared for budget cuts, the state’s governor laid out a list of options for Medicaid decreases. One of them called to cut a set of programs that help people with disabilities live in their homes. In the end, lawmakers only adopted a more narrow cut to disability care. As federal protections fade, Americans with disabilities fear a return to institutions But as Idaho’s tight budget years dwell — and the federal government softens its stance on prioritizing keeping people with disabilities in their homes instead of in institutions — disability advocates are growing worried that home care might face cuts. Expanded decades ago, home and community-based services have become a staple for state Medicaid programs. But as the Trump administration seeks to reinterpret a U.S. Supreme Court decision that serves as a foundation for expanded rights of people with disabilities to receive care in their homes, disability advocates worry that home and community-based services could be threatened. Advocates maintain that the underlying laws requiring home care options remain. The federal government’s stance — detailed in a recent memo by the U.S. Justice Department — comes before states will see the impact of massive federal Medicaid cuts enacted in President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. “When (states’) federal funding shrinks, they’re going to be reluctant to replace it with state funding, and so they will be tempted to try to reduce funding for home community-based services,” retired Idaho disability rights attorney Jim Baugh said. “But, I presume without a plan for what to do with the people who lose those services, or who have their services reduced, because we don’t have any alternative. So I just see this leaving people in the lurch. I see this being a dangerous possibility.” Several advocates also worry that there aren’t enough institutional settings to care for people with disabilities, if home and community-based services faced cuts. Earlier this year, Idaho officials estimated home and community-based services cost the state more than $176 million in state general funds, and were used by more than 16,000 Idahoans at least once a year. Most Idahoans who use home and community-based services are aging seniors who paid off their homes and want to remain there but need support, said Disability Rights Idaho Executive Director Amy Cunningham. “That’s consistent with Idaho values — that people buy homes and they live in their homes for as long as they can,” she said. “And home and community-based services allows that to happen. And it would be very sad if Idaho decided to move toward institutionalization versus allowing people to stay in their homes, in their communities, participate in community activities, participate in their community churches, be close to their families.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: A mother holds hands with her son on a swing set. At least seven states have passed laws making equally shared parenting time the legal default in child custody cases. (Photo by Troy Bennett for Maine Morning Star) A growing number of states are making an equal split between parents the default child custody option in divorce cases. Louisiana and Mississippi this year joined at least five other states that have adopted the so-called 50-50 standard — four of them since 2021, as more legislators rework divorce-related laws that remained mostly unchanged for years. The 50-50 custody issue does not break down cleanly along partisan lines: The Mississippi bill was sponsored by Republicans, the Louisiana legislation by Democrats. Both states’ laws explicitly codify a custody guideline that many courts in other states follow. Supporters say a formal 50-50 custody standard makes divorce proceedings more equitable for fathers — who historically have been awarded less custody time than mothers — and encourages them to maintain an active role in their children’s lives. And it can reduce friction between separating parents by signaling they’re both starting the custody process on an equal playing field, said Don Hubin, board chair of the National Parents Organization, an advocacy group that has pushed for more states to adopt legal presumptions of shared parenting. Without that presumption, Hubin said, one or both parents may feel like they have to paint each other in a bad light in order to ‘win’ more time with their children. “It’s not just about the practice of shared parenting, but about the law signaling to parents that this is going to be the outcome unless something special is going on in your case,” he said. “It reduces the anxiety of the parents, which reduces the conflict between the parents.” But critics say the standard might harm vulnerable women and children by making it more likely that children must spend time with a parent who isn’t safe. They fear that for women in abusive marriages, the knowledge they would have to cede 50% of their child’s time to an unsafe parent could push them to remain in a marriage just to protect their children. Kimberly Rummage, who lives in Kentucky, calls her state’s 50-50 custody standard “absolutely diabolical.” She’s had a lengthy battle in court with her ex-husband over custody of their child. “I think that parents should have to prove why they get that 50-50,” she said. “You should have to show what you’ve done in that child’s life, what you know about that child, how you’ve participated and supported that child.” Some critics also argue that the 50-50 standard doesn’t account for the needs of children at different ages. Mississippi state Rep. Dana McLean, a Republican, warned her colleagues the state’s new law could harm breastfeeding infants who need to spend most of their time with their mothers during their first months of life. Mississippi’s new law requires family courts to use equally-shared parenting time as the default in custody cases. Parents seeking more time must present evidence showing why a 50-50 split isn’t in their child’s best interest. It also changes how child support is calculated: The new formula for 50-50 custody can lower child support payments for the parent with the lower income. Louisiana’s new law says child custody “shall” be divided equally, rather than “should,” which was the language under the previous law. In both states, as in others that have adopted the 50-50 standard, a judge can override the rule if the court finds credible evidence for awarding more time to one parent. But in Mississippi, several judges spoke against the bill before it passed, saying the old system — in which custody was awarded on a case-by-case basis using a specific set of factors — was the most fair. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho revenue exceeded the state’s forecast for the month of August by $37.5 million, marking the second consecutive month in the new fiscal year where revenue beat projections, according to a new state report. Through the first two months of fiscal year 2027, which began July 1, Idaho’s revenue collections have come in $51.2 million ahead of projections, according to the August edition of the fIscal year 2027 General Fund Budget Monitor. For the month of August, strong individual income tax collections that exceeded the monthly projection by $40.8 million helped push overall revenue collections ahead of forecast. Although it is still very early in the fiscal year, Idaho is projected to end the fiscal year June 30 with a positive ending balance of $657 million if state revenue collections come in as forecasted for the remainder of the fiscal year. That would leave the state with a surplus of more than $500 million compared to the budget state legislators set. Sen. Scott Grow, R-Eagle, makes a comment during the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting on Jan. 14, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “My reaction was its very promising report, and I’m glad to see the individual income tax is up,” said Sen. Scott Grow, a Republican from Eagle who serves as co-chairman of the Idaho Legislature’s Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee. So far, the state budget picture in fiscal year 2027 looks different than a year ago, when Gov. Brad Little and the Idaho Legislature implemented a series of near-across-the-board, permanent budget cuts to pay for a series of federal and state tax cuts and ensure a balanced budget, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Grow said the increased revenue, so far, in fiscal year 2027 is good news, but he isn’t in a rush to spend any additional revenue. Grow said the Idaho Legislature may have additional, unexpected expenses and bills this year related to Medicaid, wildfire suppression, health insurance costs for state employees and the state’s corrections system that may need to be addressed. Idaho’s prisons are full. Corrections agency will request $45.3 million to open 3 new facilities. “The challenge is we always have to project a year and a half out when we are working on budgets during the legislative session, so it’s hard to know what is going to happen, which is why we try to be as conservative as we can,” Grow said. If there is still a surplus at the end of the year, Grow said he would like to discuss restoring some of last year’s transportation budget cuts. “With transportation, we had to cut that (budget) pretty skinny last year,” Grow said. “But with all (population) growth we continue to have in Idaho, hopefully we can get some money for transportation to help with the state highways – not just the maintenance, but to actually help with additional highways we need and expansion.” The Idaho Legislature is not in session, but the 2027 regular legislative session begins Jan. 11 at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. 2026-08-BudgetMonitor GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.title: Bringing Idaho’s education decisions back where they belong
items.summary: (Boise) – As a state, Idaho is often described as self-reliant and independent. We take pride in local control, including when it comes to our public education system. items.body: (Boise) – As a state, Idaho is often described as self-reliant and independent. We take pride in local control, including when it comes to our public education system. Unlike some other states, we do not look to Washington D.C. to govern our local communities. We know what we need – and how to get it done. As the U.S. Department of Education continues its work to restore state control and localize educational governance nationwide, Idaho has put itself at the forefront of making the most of an opportunity to make our public system work for Idaho students – not for students in California or Washington D.C. This is a common-sense acknowledgement that different states and communities have needs that are best understood by the people who live and serve in them. The Idaho Department of Education has recently applied for – and was granted – a federal waiver that will allow the state to make its own decisions on the spending of certain federal dollars. This work was done in response to a general complaint that when states receive federal dollars for education, they have limited authority in how to use those funds to maximize student outcomes. Now, with this federal waiver, schools are better positioned to meet local needs. Idaho is now a proud member of states granted Ed Flex waiver status and is eager to make itself a leader when it comes to state-led improvements in K-12 public education. Simply put: the federal government gives schools a set of rules to follow. An Ed-Flex waiver gives a state permission to change some of those rules if there is a better way to help students learn. There is an additional waiver to be submitted later this month. The Returning Education to the States waiver is designed to provide flexibilities that honor the principle that the people who know their students best – parents, teachers, principals, schools, and states – should have more authority to make decisions that fit their needs. The waiver brings decision making closer to students, reduces unnecessary paperwork, and allows schools to use their federal resources in a way that works for them. These waivers, in addition to reducing state and federal testing for Idaho students, should send a clear message to Idahoans about where we stand when it comes to the importance of small government and local control. Idaho will continue to strengthen its reputation as a state where families feel confident in their public schools, where taxpayers feel assurance that their dollars are being well-handled and well-spent, and where students can work towards a successful future in their own communities and beyond. This is a major victory for Idaho’s kids and further reinforces that in this state, we value prudent, conservative stewardship of taxpayer dollars. The best answers for Idaho’s schools are found around kitchen tables, in local communities, and inside Idaho classrooms. By rolling back federal overreach, protecting parental rights, and honoring local leadership, we can build an education framework that reflects Idaho values, respects local taxpayers, and equips every child in our state to succeed.

items.body: The University of Idaho could get rid of its last standardized test requirement. If the change goes into effect for fall 2027, it would bring the U of I in line with other colleges and universities in the region, a university spokeswoman said Tuesday. The proposed change also comes in the midst of an evolving national debate over standardized tests. Most colleges and universities don’t require ACT or SAT scores, and some don’t look at them at all, but some of the nation’s most selective schools are reinstating testing requirements. For the vast majority of applicants, the U of I is already test-optional . High school graduates with a GPA of 3.0 or higher are admitted automatically, with no test required. The same goes for in-state students who score proficient of higher on the Idaho Standards Achievement Test. Graduates with GPAs of 2.3 to 2.59 don’t need to submit a test score either; they enroll through the Vandal Gateway Program for first-year general studies majors. The test requirement only applies to students that fall in a donut hole — with GPAs of 2.6 to 2.99. About 11% of the U of I’s incoming class falls within this range, spokeswoman Jodi Walker said. The U of I had dropped all testing requirements during the COVID-19 pandemic. Officials began looking at the U of I’s sole testing requirement in the spring, as this year’s application season drew to a close. This year’s numbers suggest the U of I’s recent enrollment surge is slowing — and probably for a number of reasons, including a shrinking population of 18- to 22-year-olds, and a rising public debate over the value of a four-year degree. University officials decided the testing requirement was one easy lever to pull, Walker said. “The landscape is changing,” she said. “Why put up barriers that don’t necessarily need to be there?” The decision, for now, falls to interim Provost Brooke Blevins . If Blevins signs onto the proposal, the admissions change would go into effect on an interim basis, kicking off a two-year faculty review. That would give the faculty time to see if the change is having an impact on enrollment and access, Walker said. Idaho colleges and universities set their own admissions guidelines — and Boise State University, Idaho State University and Lewis-Clark State College do not require SAT and ACT scores. Standardized test mandates have fallen out of favor nationally, and are rare in the West. According to the National Center for Fair & Open Testing (FairTest), a Brooklyn, N.Y.,-based group, only 7% of colleges and universities require standardized tests . The vast majority of colleges fall into a broad category of test-optional schools — and despite the U of I’s limited testing requirement for some students, FairTest lists the U of I as test-optional. According to FairTest, all colleges in Idaho and its neighboring states are test-optional or “test-free,” which means test scores aren’t even considered in the admissions process. But all eight Ivy League colleges and universities are reinstating their pre-COVID standardized testing requirements, and other top-ranking schools are following suit, Higher Ed Dive reported in August . The schools are facing some external pressure from the Trump administration, which favors standardized testing. FairTest Executive Director Harry Feder downplayed the trend. “Ivy Plus schools, as wealthy, exclusive national outliers, have increasingly gone back to requiring test scores for admission for their own institutional reasons and in response to external pressures,” he said in a recent news release. “The national picture of test-optional and test-free admissions is actually very stable.”

items.body: The Boise School District’s enrollment is down 699 students compared to last fall, according to a report presented to the school board Monday. The 3% dip isn’t a surprise. District leaders projected and planned for a 600-student decrease when they set their budget for the current school year. And it continues a trend that started about a decade ago. Since 2015, Boise’s enrollment has dropped 22%, from 28,078 to 21,805 this fall. On Monday, district administrator Jason Hutchison gave trustees two possible reasons for the downward curve: a declining birth rate and a lack of affordable housing in Boise. While Idaho’s population is growing, fewer residents are having children. Between 2005 and 2024, the birth rate among women ages 15-44 decreased from 78.9 per 1,000 to 58.6 per 1,000, according to the National Center for Health Statistics . The slowing birth rate means fewer students entering school, and that’s been a trend across Idaho’s public schools in recent years. Between the 2021-22 and 2025-26 school years, kindergarten enrollment statewide dipped 8.5% while 12th-grade enrollment increased 9.9%. In Boise, both elementary and secondary enrollments have decreased. But younger grades have decreased at a faster rate. This fall, Boise lost 428 elementary students compared to 271 secondary students. “Anytime your seniors are outpacing your incoming kindergarten class annually, which ours have been doing … you have a gap in enrollment,” Hutchison said. There are also students who were previously enrolled in the Boise School District but left for various reasons. Exit data shows that among the students who left the district during the 2024-25 school year: 57% transferred to another public school district or public charter school 17% moved to another state 8% transferred to a homeschool setting 7% transferred to a private school. Boise trustee Alejandro Necochea on Monday asked district administrators to share with the school board more information on the students who leave midyear. “How many kids are still in our community who just dropped out of our radar?” he said. Idaho Education News previously reported that the district cut funding for 17 jobs in anticipation of the enrollment decline. Assistant Superintendent Nick Smith said Monday that district administrators will continue to watch enrollment numbers before Nov. 1 — the cutoff for fall average daily attendance, which determines state funding for employee salaries and benefits. “We do anticipate that (enrollment) will fluctuate between now and Nov. 1,” Smith said, “so we do believe that 600 number that we budgeted on is going to be pretty realistic.”

items.body: The South Idaho Correctional Institution sign outside the facility in Kuna. The facility houses about 400 women and 300 men. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Correction: This story was corrected at 9 a.m., Sept. 16 to reflect that women state prison inmates are not sent out of state due to a shortage of beds. They are sent to county jails. If a woman incarcerated at the South Idaho Correctional Institution in Kuna has a dentist appointment, she has to walk through the men’s side of the prison to attend it. To do that, correctional staff must shut down much of the men’s side, restricting everybody’s movement to get her to her appointment. There are nearly 400 women and 300 men at the medium-security prison , which was originally designed for men. South Idaho Correctional Institution Warden Jennifer Tyvand (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) South Idaho Correctional Institution Warden Jennifer Tyvand is hoping a new women’s facility, slated to open in December 2027, will help solve many of the challenges of trying to house both men and women there. The new women’s prison is one of three new facilities the Idaho Department of Correction, or IDOC, plans to open within the next year. According to a preliminary budget request, the state agency will ask Idaho legislators in January for around $45.3 million to furnish and operate those new facilities to address a statewide shortage of prison beds. The new facilities will add nearly 1,000 new beds in the state prison system. The Legislature approved funding to build the facilities, but those appropriations didn’t include funding to furnish, equip and staff each of them. In 2022, lawmakers approved $112.4 million for a new women’s prison and $37.6 million for improvements to the medical annex at the Idaho State Correctional Institution in Kuna through House Bill 791. In 2024, the Legislature appropriated $10 million for the new facility in Orofino in HB 768. Bree Derrick (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Correction) “If we don’t open them, first of all, as a state we’d have nearly $200 million of investment that’s going to sit empty,” IDOC Director Bree Derrick said at an interview at the South Idaho Correctional Institution. “… In terms of the management of the population, we would continue to essentially limp along in the same way we have done, which means probably over-reliance on county jails and on out-of-state contract beds. And then, as it relates to the women, the women will remain here for the foreseeable future.” The state is short about 200 beds for women inmates, which means some are sent to county jails, according to the agency budget request. Idaho’s entire prison population is about 10,000 inmates, according to state data , but the total prison capacity sits at just over 8,200. The agency, along with all other state agencies, submitted its budget request to the governor’s budget staff at the Division of Financial Management earlier this month. In January, Gov. Brad Little will unveil his own state budget proposal, and legislators will decide how to appropriate funds during the 2027 legislative session. IDOC to request $32.9M to open new women’s prison Idaho incarcerates women at the highest rate in the nation, according to the most recent available data from the U.S. Department of Justice. The state began housing women in the Kuna men’s prison in 2012 because the Kuna women’s prison was full. “We struggle to provide them the same types of opportunities that we do for our male population,” Tyvand said. The women at the facility don’t have access to the ballfields on their side and have more limited classroom and work-training space, she said. The women also live in open areas with bunk beds placed close together, including in the area meant to be the least restrictive. Tyvand said the structure isn’t as “incentivized” as it should be. Cameron told lawmakers that the rise was partly because the company had recently taken over the state contract, and partly because the state had banned covering prescription medication for weight loss in late 2025. items.body: A quarterly report and an independent audit tell conflicting stories about the Idaho School Benefit Trust’s finances, according to public documents shared by the Idaho Department of Insurance last week. Meanwhile, included in those documents, internal board minutes show the trust painted a rosy picture of low rates and stability and unveil that the trust paid out $1.9 million on a single claim, shedding light on why some claims exceeded expectations this past year. The department is investigating what led to the trust’s collapse and has petitioned the court to take over and rehabilitate the self-funded health care plan that pays medical claims for thousands of public school employees and dependents. As of Tuesday, Fourth District Court Judge Lynn Norton has not yet approved the department’s request. “We understand that districts and other interested parties want answers now, and we ask for the opportunity to complete the examination and its determinations before drawing conclusions,” department spokesperson Julie Robinson wrote in a Monday email to EdNews. After receiving multiple records requests, the department last week posted 11 documents totaling 152 pages on its web page dedicated to sharing information about the trust. It needed a minimum of $8.2 million in surplus and had $13.5 million, an excess of $5.3 million. After two years of losses totaling $7.3 million, the trust appeared to be having a good year. items.title: We can’t stop Idaho from growing, but with more housing options, we can choose how
items.summary: In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening, writes guest columnist Ali Rabe. (Photo by Getty Images) Every week, public hearings across the Treasure Valley and beyond fill up with an emerging voice: residents, many of whom moved here in the last five to ten years, showing up to vote down
items.body: In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening, writes guest columnist Ali Rabe. (Photo by Getty Images) Every week, public hearings across the Treasure Valley and beyond fill up with an emerging voice: residents, many of whom moved here in the last five to ten years, showing up to vote down housing options their communities need. They organize, vote, and pressure local officials to reject more housing. I understand where that instinct comes from. I just don’t think it’s pointing us toward the right answer. Idaho leads the nation in housing growth. The data shows it’s still not enough. I grew up in Middleton, surrounded by farm fields. Those fields are gone now, replaced by one-acre lots with little infrastructure to support them. I’ve watched Idaho change in ways that make me sad, and I understand the anti-growth mindset. Too often growth here has meant sprawl, distant subdivisions, and longer commutes. But growth itself isn’t the enemy. Communities grow and change, and that change can make a place better, not worse. The Treasure Valley will keep growing. The question is how. During my nearly seven years leading Jesse Tree , the Treasure Valley’s eviction prevention nonprofit, I watched more and more Idahoans lose their footing here. People who worked full time couldn’t make rent, families were evicted, and some ended up homeless. In recent years, eviction and homelessness doubled as regional housing costs climbed roughly 40%, and the gap between wages and home prices keeps widening. Meanwhile, most of what gets built on our fringe is the same product: large-lot homes pushing half a million dollars, aimed at out-of-state buyers. Young Idahoans, our workforce, and longtime locals are left out. There’s a better path, and it isn’t new. It’s called missing middle housing, and it’s a return to how Idaho used to build. Missing middle housing means duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes, cottage courts, and small-lot homes woven into existing neighborhoods rather than dropped onto the fringe. It’s gentle, incremental density that adds homes without ruining a neighborhood’s character. Look at Idaho’s historic neighborhoods and you’ll find these home types everywhere. This is how our cities grew before exclusionary zoning took hold in the 1970s and made large-lot sprawl the only easy path for developers. It’s also better economics, for residents and for cities. Land is the single largest cost on a developer’s pro forma. When zoning only allows large-lot product, that cost gets baked into every home, which is why half-million-dollar houses keep getting built. Smaller homes on smaller lots bring that cost down and open the door to starter homes again. For cities, more homes per acre means more property value per acre without miles of new pipes, roads, and schools. It’s a better deal for taxpayers on both ends. None of this requires upending the neighborhoods people love. In my experience, when people see what missing middle housing actually is, rather than what they assume it is, most come around. Even hearing opponents soften once they realize it isn’t a five-story apartment complex next door. It’s a duplex that looks like the house beside it. I don’t fault anyone for wanting to protect what they love about this place. I love it too, farm fields and all. But protecting Idaho doesn’t mean freezing it in place, and it certainly doesn’t mean a housing market that only works for people who aren’t from here. It means asking a better question: how do we grow in a way that gives our young people, our workforce, and our own neighbors a shot at homeownership? Missing middle housing is one of the clearest answers we have. If you want to help make the case in your community, Gem State Housing Alliance is activating pro-housing voices across the state, and we’d love to welcome you. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.body: An Alaska Airlines jet lands at Newark Liberty International Airport. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor) One of my earliest memories is sitting behind my dad in his airplane, pressing my face to the window, watching the big buildings shrink to look like Lego sets. I remember thinking: I want to fly a plane one day. The memories of flying with my dad – a fixed wing and helicopter pilot who repaired power lines – stayed with me for years of raising three wonderful children and working in sales. It wasn’t until my early 40s that I completed my private pilot license, the first step in my pilot career. I’m currently completing my instrument rating while working toward my commercial certificate, both needed to achieve my long-term goal of building a career in corporate aviation. My story matters now because women don’t need to wait until mid-life to become pilots. If the calling comes in childhood, follow it. Girls in Aviation Day returns to Boise on Saturday, Sept. 19, and I want as many people as possible, especially girls who may assume a cockpit isn’t for them, to see what’s possible. Women hold only about 5.5% to 6% of U.S. airline pilot jobs. This number has barely moved in decades, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Meanwhile, North American airlines expect to be 30,000 pilots short of what they need by 2032, despite the U.S. government projecting that there will be roughly 18,000 new airline and commercial pilot openings this decade. My timeline was unusual and now I’m training while balancing significant family responsibilities that don’t pause for flight lessons. Training is expensive, and self-funding my dream has meant real sacrifice for myself and my family. I’ve asked myself more than once whether it made sense to keep going. My answer has stayed the same: yes. I credit that to the mentorship I’ve received from other women in aviation. A scholarship through Women in Corporate Aviation last year helped me pass my instrument written exam and keep training toward my checkride. I pay it forward by mentoring girls through our local chapter of Women in Aviation and volunteering with events like Girls in Aviation Day, because I wouldn’t be here without seeing the many women before me who have made it to the rank of captain. Girls in Aviation Day brings around 250 girls ages 8 to 18 to Western Aircraft in Boise for a free day of aircraft tours, hands-on activities, and one-on-one time with women working across aviation and aerospace: pilots, engineers, mechanics, dispatchers, air traffic controllers. For many of these girls, it may be the first time they see someone who looks like them doing this job. Representation changes what a kid believes is possible for herself. While I didn’t have many women pilots to point to when I was younger, those in my life are instrumental in keeping me on my career path. I want the girls in the Treasure Valley community to have that now, not decades later. I want women considering aviation later in life, like I did, to know their timeline doesn’t have to look a certain way. Please bring the girls in your life to Western Aircraft at the Boise Airport between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. Registration is free at bit.ly/GIAD2026 . items.body: Idaho State Superintendent of Public Instruction Debbie Critchfield, a Republican running for another term in November, speaks to an attendee after a candidate forum on Aug. 4, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Sean Dolan/EdNews) This story was originally posted on IdahoEdNews.org on Sept. 10, 2026. Debbie Critchfield wants $20 million to help school districts and charters keep pace with inflation, and support at-risk students. Even if the 2027 Legislature signs on, the $20 million would get carved up quickly. But the state superintendent said she prefers to enter the next session with a workable request, and not one that is immediately dismissed as “ridiculous.” “I’d rather ask for something that I believe we can get to,” Critchfield said Wednesday. After budget cuts, Idaho plans to maintain low government spending, state official says In an EdNews interview, Critchfield discussed the 2027-28 spending request she submitted a week ago — and the political calculus that went into her budget. All told, Critchfield is seeking more than $3.3 billion for K-12, a 3.9% increase. But her one new budget request is a $20 million slice of the pie. She wants this increase to go into “operational” spending — commonly called discretionary funds, because districts and charters can use this line item for any purpose. And that makes it a popular request in the K-12 community, Critchfield said Wednesday. So far, she said, she has heard only positive feedback from school administrators. “(It’s) the most flexible and customizable part of the budget for districts and charters.” However, there also would be a lot of pressure on the $20 million. Operational funding, now at $366 million, has essentially been frozen for three years. An increase could help address inflation. Schools could also use the increase to cover unexpected bills from the Idaho School Benefit Trust. Districts and charters are on the hook for much of the trust’s $13 million shortfall — and as EdNews reported this week, employee medical claims could be denied if a member of the trust refuses to pay their share of the $13 million. The trust shortfall came to light in July, but Critchfield’s budget has no money to address it directly. Lastly, the new operational money could support a rewrite of Idaho’s aging school funding formula. Idaho politicians have long discussed changes to the formula, adopted in 1994. Supporters of a rewrite, including Critchfield, want to provide extra funding to support at-risk students, such as special education students. While $20 million won’t cover a new formula entirely, it could provide first-year funding, Critchfield said Wednesday. Dedicated dollars could smooth the transition, covering schools that would lose money under a new formula. And this would be a departure from 2025, when lawmakers debated a funding formula bill that had no dollars attached to it. While Critchfield is pushing the $20 million line item, the Republican is seeking less money for the special education program she navigated through the 2026 Legislature. Her budget contains $1.7 million for a “high-needs” fund, for students who require full-time staff support or costly equipment. This year’s high-needs budget is $5 million. items.summary: Wildfire smoke rolls over the skies near Warm Springs along U.S. Highway 26 on July 25, 2026. (Photo by Oregon Department of Transportation) Oregon lawmakers approved nearly $123 million to help cover the costs of this year’s wildfire season, sending money to two state agencies responsible for fighting wildfires. The Oregon Legislature’s Joint Emergency Board agreed to allocate $108 million to the
items.body: Wildfire smoke rolls over the skies near Warm Springs along U.S. Highway 26 on July 25, 2026. (Photo by Oregon Department of Transportation) Oregon lawmakers approved nearly $123 million to help cover the costs of this year’s wildfire season, sending money to two state agencies responsible for fighting wildfires. The Oregon Legislature’s Joint Emergency Board agreed to allocate $108 million to the Oregon Department of Forestry and $15 million to the Department of the State Fire Marshal at a morning meeting Thursday. The 20-member board has the authority to allocate funding when the full Legislature isn’t in session. As of late August, wildfires had scorched across 2.5 million acres and cost the state $236.2 million. Those costs are expected to reach $350 million by the end of the wildfire season — putting 2026 on track to surpass the state’s previous $318 million record when wildfires scorched 1.9 million acres in 2024. The forestry department has been able to pay for nearly $79 million of those costs with federal recovery funding, grants and other contributions. With the emergency board’s approval Thursday, the agency will also borrow $150 million from the Oregon State Treasury through three loans over the next three months to maintain solvency through the end of the year. The State Fire Marshal responded to 12 destructive wildfires this year that cost more than $50 million. The agency’s $15 million request will cover funding gaps needed to address those costs. The federal government is expected to reimburse Oregon for some of these costs, though that money can take years to arrive. The Federal Emergency Management Agency still owes Oregon about $92 million in fire management and public assistance grants from 2020. These are grants a state requests if they are facing a catastrophic emergency, and the federal government agrees to pay 75% of the costs. Typically they take about two to three years to be fully released to the states. This is not an unusual amount of money owed, nor is it unusual that it’s taking so long to be reimbursed, according to Joy Krawczyk, a spokesperson for the Oregon Department of Forestry. The slow pace of federal reimbursements frustrated lawmakers. “Through the course of today’s allocations, we’re going to be taking general fund dollars away from our schools, from healthcare, from housing, from public safety, while we’re waiting for reimbursement from the federal government,” said Rep. David Gomberg, D-Otis. Lawmakers on the emergency board thanked all the agencies who worked to put out the wildfires this summer. “It was predicted to be tough,” said Rep. Mark Owens, R-Crane. “We exceeded tough by many levels in that period of time. Without the coordination, the dedication of the state agencies, and I’ll say our Bureau of Land Management, the U.S. Forest Service, Rangeland Fire Protection Associations, rural fire districts and the volunteers that are out there, there’d have been towns and houses taken out.” Oregon Capital Chronicle senior reporter Alex Baumhardt contributed to this story.
